questions.q: What was the author's experience with a physics class in their Civil Engineering program?
a: It focused on light and relativity and was required for accreditation
It was optional but recommended for engineering students
It covered thermodynamics needed for structural analysis
It was a lab-based course on fluid dynamics
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes the author taking a physics class on light and relativity, told by the dean it was required for accreditation.

questions.q: According to the book, why do college graduates earn higher salaries?
a: The degree signals that they possess hardworking character traits
The classroom training makes them more skilled employees
They develop new technical abilities during their studies
Employers pay more because graduates have broader knowledge
questions.why: Lesson 2 explains that the diploma is evidence of pre-existing character traits, not that school builds them.

questions.q: What is human capital theory described as in the book?
a: A flawed system that explains why graduates earn more
A proven model of workforce productivity
A government policy on education funding
A method for measuring job satisfaction
questions.why: Lesson 2 calls human capital theory a flawed system used by economists to explain the wage gap.

questions.q: What does the book suggest as a first step to fixing education?
a: Abandoning the belief that more education is always better than none
Increasing government funding for public schools
Making all college courses directly job-related
Replacing traditional grading with project-based assessment
questions.why: Lesson 3 states we need to forsake the misguided idea that it is always better to have more education.

questions.q: What did the dean tell the author when asked about the useless physics class?
a: That it was required for the program to be accredited
That it would prove useful in the long run
That the curriculum was under review for changes
That it was a personal choice by the department
questions.why: Lesson 1 recounts the author asking the dean in an exit interview and being told it was an accreditation requirement.
